# ԳԻՐՔ ԵՐԿՐՈՐԴ

Պատճառս կեցոց վախճանին Թադէոսին Հրամանոց Մանուէլի.
Եւ Սրբոյ Կաթողիկոսացն Հայոց՝ Ներսիսի և Գրիգորի խնդրին՝
զոր գրեցին առ միմեանս.

Մարգարէն Դաւիթ յԱստուածային երգսն սաղմոսացն օրհնաբանէ, եթէ յիշատակ յաւիտենից եղիցի արդարն, և Սողոմոն ասէ՝ թէ յիշատակ արդարոց՝ հանդերձ գովութբ: Յայտ առնելով՝ զի թէպէտ և հասարակական վախճանաւն փոխի յաստեացս, սակայն արձան մշտնջենաւոր ինքեան թողու յերկրի՝ զարժանի յիշատակի գործս, որով և յազգս ազգաց՝ անյապաղ՝ գովասանական երգով պատուի:

Օգտ տեսեալ մեր՝ ի նուազեալս ժամանակի՝ Հայաստանեայց Եկեղեցւոյ Առաջնորդս, ոչ յապաղիմք՝ յապա թողուլ զյիշատակ անուան նոցա, պարագրութբ բանի՝ ի հանդերձեալ ժողովուրդսն՝ որք զկնի մեր լինիցին: Զի և սոցայս՝ ախորժելի կարծեմ պատմութիւն, քան զնախ եղելոց՝ համապատիւ նոցա՝ սրբոց: Որպէս և զկնի ամպոյ՝ Արեգական, և յետ ձմերայնոյն՝ գարնանային յօդոցն քաղցրութիւն:

Այսպէս և Երանելի Հայրս՝ ի նուազեալ ժամանակս՝

<vocab>Դաւիթ (David), Սողոմոն (Solomon), Հայաստանեայց Եկեղեցի (Armenian Church), Կաթողիկոս (Catholicos), Ներսէս (Nerses), Գրիգոր (Grigor), Մանուէլ (Manuel), Թադէոս (Thaddeus), յիշատակ (remembrance/memory), սաղմոս (psalm)</vocab>
right.translation:
# BOOK TWO

The reason for the end of the writings of Thaddeus <note>A reference to the legacy of the Apostle Thaddeus</note> and the commands of Manuel. And the request of the Holy Catholicoses of Armenia, Nerses and Grigor, regarding what they wrote to one another.

The prophet David praises in his divine songs of the psalms that the memory of the righteous shall be everlasting, and Solomon says that the memory of the righteous is accompanied by praise. He reveals that although one is changed by a common end in these worldly matters, yet they leave behind an eternal monument on earth, works worthy of remembrance, for which they are honored among nations without delay with songs of praise.

Seeing the benefit in these diminished times, we, the leaders of the Armenian Church, do not delay in leaving behind the memory of their names, by describing in words for the coming generations who shall be after us. For I believe this history is as desirable and equal in honor to the saints who came before. Just as after a cloud comes the Sun, and after winter comes the sweetness of spring weather.

In this way, our blessed Father, in these diminished times,

<summary>This page introduces Book Two of the manuscript, focusing on the historical importance of preserving the memory of the righteous, specifically the Armenian Catholicoses Nerses and Grigor.</summary>
<keywords>Book Two, Nerses, Grigor, memory, righteousness, Armenian Church</keywords>

༄༅། །ལས་ལས་སོ་སོར་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག །འགྲོས་དགོས་པའི་ཡི་དྭགས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ལ་བཞག་པར་མྱོང་བར་སྐྱེའོ། །ཡོངས་སུ་སྐྱེ་བའི་མཐའ་སྐྱེ་བས་དེ་ཆགས་པས་སྐྱེའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ལས་ལ་སྐྱེ་བས་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ། །མཐའ་གྱིས་བསམ་པའི་བསམ་པ་ལ་དཔྱད་རྫོགས་སོ། །དེ་བས་བདག་གི་བདག་གནས་སུ་བཅོམ་པར་བསྟེན་པའི་བསམ་པ་སྟེ་བསམ་པའི་བསམ་པ་མཐའ་བའི་རིམ་པར་ལྡན་རྫོགས་སོ། །དེ་བས་བདག་གི་བདག་ཅེས་པའི་བདག་དེ་བས་དཔྱད་རྫོགས་སོ། །རྣམ་པར་བདག་པའི་བསམ་མི་ཚད་པའི་དེ་ཉིད་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་དཔྱད་རྫོགས་སོ། །རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་མ་ལས་བདག་གི་བསམ་པ་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་རིམ་པར་ནི་བསམ། །རྣམ་པར་བསམ་པ་ནས་དཔྱད་རྫོགས་པས་མཐའ་སྐྱེ། །གཞན་དུ་སྐྱེ་བར་མཐའ་བཅད་པར་ལས་སུ་རྟོགས་སོ། །དེ་ཅི་ཕྱིར་ཞེན། །བསམ་པ་རྣམས་ལ་བདག་གིས་བསམ་པའི་བསམ་པ་ཅན་གྱི་བསམ་པ་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མཐའ་ཅན་དེ་བས་མ ### Top Section

The self-born mother <note>original: rang skyes ma; a metaphorical reference to innate wisdom or the source of reality</note> does not change karma through itself. Through assembly, a single karma is born from the aggregation. In that way, by being born, one is born beyond the nature of the finite. By being born through assembly, one goes beyond the limit of birth and suppresses the limit of assembly. Why is it appropriate to regard the self in this way? Therefore, the specific realities that depend on karma are distinct. Furthermore, why does the finite individual see the self as complete through conditions? The self is also like that. Why is that self conceptualized? The knot <note>referring to the knots of ignorance or habitual tendencies</note> is conceptualized in such a manner. Why are others conceptualized? Why is there a conceptualizing self? With the self that descends, gods, humans, sentient beings, hungry ghosts <term>preta</term> <gloss>beings in a state of constant craving and suffering due to past greed</gloss>, the animal realm, the great, and the small exist as goddesses and forms. Therefore, why is it like the limit of the self? Regarding the so-called self, what is the activity of the so-called finite self? The activity of all is limitless and powerful. Therefore, what is perceived is clear. Why is it called the finite? Therefore, regarding the so-called finite self, what is the activity?

### Bottom Section

One conceptualizes separately based on karma. The experience of the hungry ghost mind, which requires movement, is born. Through the birth of the limit of total birth, it is born through attachment. Thus, being born into karma, it is likewise. The investigation of the intention of intentions is complete. Therefore, the intention that relies on the destruction of the self's dwelling place is the intention of intentions; it is complete in its connection to the sequence of the finite. Therefore, the analysis of the self called the self's self is complete. The investigation into the immeasurable reality of the perfectly pure self of sentient beings is complete. Son of noble family, think sequentially regarding those who possess the intention of the self. From the investigation of the conceptualization being complete, the limit is born. In being born elsewhere, the limit is cut and understood as karma. Why is that? རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བསྡུས་པའི་རྒྱུ་རྣམ་པར་གཉིས་ཡིན་ཏེ། །གཉིས་པ་དང་། །སྒྲུབ་དང་། །ཚོགས་རྐྱེན་ག། །གཞན་ཡང་དེ་ལྟར་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་གནས་མཆོག་དམ་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །སྡུས་བསྡུས་པ་རྣམ་པར་རིག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་སོགས་མཐའ་ཡས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བཞི་པའི་དགེ་སློང་། །དེ་ལྟར་བཅུ་བས་དཔའ་བརྩོན་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཟླ་བའི་ལྟ་བ་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །དེ་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ན། །སྒྲ་མཚན་དུ་ལས་སུ་རུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྒྲ་མཚན་དུ་ལས་སུ་རུང་བའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་དེ་དག་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །བདག་ཉིད་དེ་དག་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །བདག་ཉིད་དེ་དག་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །དེ་ལྟར་དད་པའི་ལས་བསྒྲུབ། །གཅིག་ཏུ་མཚན་པས་ཟླ་བ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་སོ། །གཟུགས་མེད་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་སོ། །རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་དེ་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་སོ། །བསྒྲུབ་པའང་། །མཚན་པས་མཐོང་བའོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བདག་ཉིད་བཞི་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གྱི་སེམས་པ་བཞིན་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གྱི་སེམས་པ་བཞིན་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །རྣམ་པར་དཔྱད་པར་བྱའོ། །རྣམ་པར་དཔྱད་པའོ། །

མི་དགེ་བའི་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །གཞན་ཡང་མཁས་པས་བཞེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་རྣམ་པར་དེ་ཉིད་རྣམ་པར་ཡིན་ལ། །མི་དགེ་བའི་དགེ་སློང་རྣམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་རྣམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །མཁས་པས་བཞེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །དཔྱད་བཅས་པའི་ལས་བསྒྲུབ། །མཚན་པས་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ལས་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །མི་དགེ་བའི་མཚན་པས་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་མཚན་པས་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །གཞན་ཡང་ཚོགས་པ་བཅས་པའི་རྣམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །གཅིག་གི་ཚིག་ཏུ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །དེ་ལྟར་གྱི་སེམས་པ་བཞིན་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གྱི་སེམས་པ་བཞིན་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །གཅིག་ཏུ་མཚན་པས་ཟླ་བ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །མཁས་པས་བཞེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ། །གཞན་ཡང་ཚོགས་པ་བཅས་པའི་རྣམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པའོ། །

まのあつさかちこくのあはれさも

きみの行事とて陸奥へ

のまのくは其妻や子の宿とほき

left.translation:
The sleeve of the man, having come from Hama-Tateyama, <note>a sacred mountain site</note>
The depth of the mountain and the pathos of these far-off provinces,
Thinking of the heart of the person who lingers in my thoughts,
Oh, the mountain path is filled with a myriad of sorrows.
As the night deepens along the treacherous and rugged path,
Abandoned to the resentment of a dreamless sleep, the mountain foot
Is adorned with chrysanthemums <note>original: "kiku"</note> in the cooling air of early autumn.

<column-break/>

This is his task as he journeys toward Mutsu.
Since it is a journey into the unknown, he is deeply moved
By the words of the person at the shore who speaks of the sorrows of autumn.
He thinks of his distant wife and child at home,
Gathering up the pathos of his departure,
He heads toward this place, unexpected and unforeseen,
Wiping his sleeves as he contemplates the chill of early autumn.

<summary>A traveler reflects on the sorrow and loneliness of his journey toward the province of Mutsu, feeling the weight of the autumn season and the separation from his family.</summary>
<keywords>Mutsu, Hama-Tateyama, travel, autumn, sorrow, separation</keywords>

left.translation:
The text continues the theme of spiritual devotion and ascetic discipline, transitioning from general exhortations on repentance to specific teachings attributed to Saint Ephrem the Syrian. A small, dark, elongated stain or possibly a wax drop appears on the left side of the middle section of the page, partially obscuring a few characters. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Because from Him is known the power of God, who is always near to us, and we find Him in all times and seasons, as the prophet said: "The Lord is near to all those who call upon Him in truth and in right faith." Let us not let His mercies and His grace depart from us. Amen. And again, because He desires that all human beings be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, for this reason He has given us a time of repentance and forgiveness, so that we may all turn from our evil ways and live by His grace. And now, my beloved brothers, I have desired to write for you from the words of the holy fathers, so that they may be for our help and for the healing of our souls and our bodies, and for the rest of our spirit, so that we may please God in all our labors. And one of the holy ones said: "Those who love God with all their heart and with all their mind, they cannot be idle from prayer and from the praise of God at any time." And again he said: "Prayer is the mother of all good things, and it is that which brings a human being to God, and it grants him life eternal." And for this reason, it is right for us to be diligent in prayer and in petition through all the days of our lives, so that we may be worthy of the mercies of our Lord. And again he said: "Whoever desires to be purified from evil passions and from hateful thoughts, let him be constant in the reading of the holy scriptures and in prayer by night and by day." And thus he shall find rest for his soul and his body in this world and in that which is to come, through the prayers of all the saints. Amen.
->Again from the words of Mar Ephrem<- O human being, fear God and do His commandments at all times. And do not be negligent in your life, but remember the day of death. And that hour when your soul shall depart from your body and stand before the judgment of the living God, and give an account of everything that you did in this world. This page contains a pastoral exhortation on the necessity of constant prayer, repentance, and the study of scripture for spiritual healing, followed by a short meditative excerpt attributed to Ephrem the Syrian regarding the final judgment. <meta>The source language provided in the instructions was Hebrew and Judeo-Arabic, but the OCR text is Syriac. The translation is based on the Syriac manuscript text. The page continues from the previous discussion on the prayers of the holy ones.</meta>

<warning>The manuscript shows significant aging, with ink bleed-through from the reverse side, some staining, and wormholes affecting legibility in several areas.</warning>

<margin></margin>
<unclear>...to him</unclear>
<unclear>...a</unclear>
</margin>

If, however, it is changed, repeated, and recognized from person <term>parsopa</term> <gloss>person or hypostasis</gloss> to person.
As we see that from the Holy One <note>referring to the Divine</note> what is created is one and does not change.
As the Fathers <note>original: "abahata"</note> also said, just as the person <note>original: "parsopa"</note> of the Word <term>Milta</term> <gloss>the Divine Word or Logos</gloss> is one.
Yet sometimes they say that it is changed from one to another among human beings.
And when we see that it is one and does not change, as the Fathers also said.

<note>The remainder of the page consists of the repeated iteration of the preceding theological statements. The text focuses on the unity and immutability of the Divine Word in contrast to the changing nature of human persons. This repetition likely serves a mnemonic or liturgical purpose within the manuscript.</note>

<summary>This page presents a repetitive theological argument regarding the nature of the Divine Word. It asserts that the hypostasis of the Word is a singular, unchanging unity as taught by the Church Fathers.</summary>

And thus, like the simple proclamation of the word of the cross, to those who are perishing it is foolishness, but to us who are being saved, it is the power of God. Even if at the time it was not salvation, it is a new and glorious salvation that is called by that which was known from before. And this is what Paul said: how is it new, if to those who are perishing it is foolishness, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God? When it is right to know that even if at the time of Moses it was, from the time of the forefathers, salvation from the fear of God, but the salvation of the Messiah from sin and from death is, and of such as this, from before it was not. And not even one of these was like this new thing. And even if at the time of the forefathers it was, but not like this. And at the time of Moses it was, but not like this. And at the time of the prophets it was, but not like this. And so, even at the time of John the Baptist it was, but not like this. Because this is new and glorious from all of them. Because this frees us from sin and from death. And as the prophets proclaimed from before about it, also John proclaimed about it. And he said that as the prophets proclaimed about the coming of the Messiah, so also John proclaimed about his coming. As the prophets proclaimed about his baptism, so also John proclaimed about his baptism. As the prophets proclaimed about his suffering, and about his burial, and about his resurrection, so also John proclaimed about them. And even if they proclaimed about them from before, but this is new and glorious. Because this is not like those that were from before. But this is new and glorious from all of them. Because this frees us from sin and from death. And this is the newness that Paul said to it, as we said from above, how it is.

<summary>The text reflects on the new and transformative nature of salvation through Christ compared to the prophetic traditions of the past, citing Paul and John the Baptist.</summary>
<keywords>Salvation, Messiah, Paul, John the Baptist, sin, death, cross, prophecy</keywords>

->Paragraph Thirty-Five<-

By this rule <note>original: "qanona"</note> we are to know whether it is manifest in the human body for the soul to be seen or not. And although we demonstrate by this law <note>original: "nomosa"</note> whether the soul is seen in the body or not in this time in which we exist; so that we may know how the soul is in this time in which we exist. And how the soul is in this time in which we exist. And how the soul is in this time in which we exist. And how the soul is in this time in which we exist. And how the soul is in this time in which we exist. And how the soul is in this time in which we exist. 

<warning>The remainder of the transcription for this page consists of the phrase "And how the soul is in this time in which we exist" repeated over one hundred times. This appears to be a major error in the OCR or a repetitive scribal exercise in the original manuscript.</warning>

<summary>This page begins an inquiry into the visibility or manifestation of the soul within the physical human body during the present time. The text quickly breaks into a repetitive loop of a single philosophical question.</summary>

פִּקְדּוּ מוֹ מָא אֲמַר לָהּ מוֹסֵי אֵי בָא בְּלִבָּא לְמֶעְבַּד
וְתִקְדַּם גְּמִירָהּ לְגִמְעוּ וּוּפְקוּ בֵּין יְדֵי אֵלָהּ וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה
זֶה הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה תַּעֲשׂוּ וְיֵרָא אֲלֵיכֶם כְּבוֹד
יְהוָה: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לִיוּ פִּתְגָּמָא דְּפַקֵּיד יְיָ תַּעְבְּדוּן
וְיִתְגְּלֵי לְכוֹן יְקָרָא דַּיְיָ: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל אַהֲרֹן קְרַב
אֶל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וַעֲשֵׂה אֶת חַטָּאתְךָ וְאֶת עֹלָתֶךָ וְכַפֵּר בַּעַדְךָ וּבְעַד הָעָם
וַעֲשֵׂה אֶת קָרְבַּן הָעָם וְכַפֵּר בַּעֲדָם כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה
יְהוָה: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה לְאַהֲרֹן קְרַב לְמַדְבְּחָא וַעֲבֵיד
יָת חַטָּאתָךְ וְיָת עֲלָתָךְ וְכַפַּר עֲלָךְ וְעַל עַמָּא וַעֲבֵיד
יָת קוּרְבַּן עַמָּא וְכַפַּר עֲלֵיהוֹן כְּמָא דְּפַקֵּיד יְיָ: וַיִּקְרַב
אַהֲרֹן אֶל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וַיִּשְׁחַט אֶת עֵגֶל הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לוֹ: וּקְרֵיב אַהֲרֹן
לְמַדְבְּחָא וּנְכַס יָת עִגְלָא דְּחַטָּאתָא דִּילֵיהּ: וַיַּקְרִבוּ
בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן אֶת הַדָּם אֵלָיו וַיִּטְבֹּל אֶצְבָּעוֹ בַּדָּם וַיִּתֵּן
עַל קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְאֶת הַדָּם יָצַק אֶל יְסוֹד הַמִּזְבֵּחַ:
וְקָרִיבוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן יָת דְּמָא לֵיהּ וּטְבַל אֶצְבְּעֵיהּ בִּדְמָא
וִיהַב עַל קַרְנַת מַדְבְּחָא וְיָת דְּמָא אֲרִיק לִיסוֹדָא
דְּמַדְבְּחָא: וְאֶת הַחֵלֶב וְאֶת הַכְּלָיֹת וְאֶת הַיֹּתֶרֶת
מִן הַכָּבֵד מִן הַחַטָּאת הִקְטִיר הַמִּזְבֵּחָה כַּאֲשֶׁר
צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה: וְיָת תַּרְבָּא וְיָת כִּלְיָתָא וְיָת
חַצְרָא מִן כַּבְדָּא מִן חַטָּאתָא אַסִּיק לְמַדְבְּחָא כְּמָא
דְּפַקֵּיד יְיָ יָת מֹשֶׁה: וְאֶת הַבָּשָׂר וְאֶת הָעוֹר שָׂרַף בָּאֵשׁ מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה:
וְיָת בִּסְרָא וְיָת מַשְׁכָּא אוֹקִיד בְּנוּרָא מִבָּרָא
לְמַשְׁרִיתָא: וַיִּשְׁחַט אֶת הָעֹלָה וַיַּמְצִאוּ בְּנֵי
אַהֲרֹן אֵלָיו אֶת הַדָּם וַיִּזְרְקֵהוּ עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ סָבִיב:
וּנְכַס יָת עֲלָתָא וְאַמְטִיאוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן לֵיהּ יָת
דְּמָא וּדְרַק עַל מַדְבְּחָא סְחוֹר סְחוֹר: וְאֶת הָעֹלָה
הִמְצִיאוּ אֵלָיו לִנְתָחֶיהָ וְאֶת הָרֹאשׁ וַיַּקְטֵר עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ:
וְיָת עֲלָתָא אַמְטִיאוּ לֵיהּ לְאֵבְרָהָא וְיָת רֵישָׁא וְאַסִּיק
עַל מַדְבְּחָא: וַיִּרְחַץ אֶת הַקֶּרֶב וְאֶת הַכְּרָעָיִם וַיַּקְטֵר עַל הָעֹלָה הַמִּזְבֵּחָה:
וְחַלִּיל יָת גַּוָּא וְיָת כְּרָעַיָּא וְאַסִּיק עַל עֲלָתָא לְמַדְבְּחָא: וַיַּקְרֵב
אֵת קָרְבַּן הָעָם וַיִּקַּח אֶת שְׂעִיר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לָעָם
וַיִּשְׁחָטֵהוּ וַיְחַטְּאֵהוּ כָּרִאשׁוֹן: וְקָרִיב יָת קוּרְבַּן עַמָּא
וּנְסֵיב יָת צְפִירָא דְּחַטָּאתָא דִּלְעַמָּא וּנְכַסֵיהּ וְכַפַּר

And he said to them, Moses said, "It has come into my heart to do, and may the completion precede the mixture/gathering." And they brought it before the Lord. And Moses said, "This is the thing which the Lord commanded that you should do; and the glory of the Lord shall appear to you." And Moses said, "This is the word that the Lord commanded: you shall do, and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed to you." And Moses said to Aaron, "Approach the altar and perform your sin offering and your burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself and for the people; and perform the offering of the people, and make atonement for them, as the Lord commanded." And Moses said to Aaron, "Approach the altar and perform your sin offering and your burnt offering, and atone for yourself and for the people, and perform the offering of the people, and atone for them, as the Lord commanded." And Aaron approached the altar and slaughtered the calf of the sin offering which was his. And Aaron approached the altar and slaughtered the calf of the sin offering that was his. And the sons of Aaron brought the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and put it on the corners of the altar, and the blood he poured out at the base of the altar. And the sons of Aaron brought the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and placed it on the corners of the altar, and the blood he poured to the base of the altar. And the fat and the kidneys and the covering from the liver from the sin offering he caused to ascend upon the altar, as the Lord commanded Moses. And the suet and the kidneys and the covering from the liver from the sin offering he brought up to the altar, as the Lord commanded Moses. And the flesh and the skin he burned with fire outside the camp. And the flesh and the skin he burned with fire outside the camp. And he slaughtered the burnt offering, and the sons of Aaron brought to him the blood, and he threw it upon the altar all around. And he slaughtered the burnt offering, and the sons of Aaron brought to him the blood, and he threw it upon the altar all around. And the burnt offering they brought to him by its pieces, and the head, and he caused it to ascend upon the altar. And the burnt offering they brought to him for its limbs, and the head, and he brought it up to the altar. And he washed the inner parts and the legs, and he caused them to ascend upon the burnt offering on the altar. And he cleansed the innards and the legs and brought them up upon the burnt offering to the altar. And he brought the offering of the people, and he took the goat of the sin offering which was for the people, and he slaughtered it and made atonement with it, like the first. And he brought the offering of the people, and he took the goat of the sin offering that was for the people, and slaughtered it and atoned...

<column-break/>

<insert></insert>
He said to him: "Approach." Tomorrow, [is it not?] the Lord is your glory, and it shall be laden with blessing. Just as the descent [of the fire] corresponds to the service of the Holy One. <note>The text suggests that the appearance of the Divine Presence is a direct result of the successful performance of the cultic service.</note>
Eight [days]—it corresponds to the service of the Holy One. For this [reason] Moses turned; he washed with Aaron. He turned from the altar. Why? Because when Aaron saw that all the offerings had been brought, and all the deeds had been completed, and the <term>Peninah</term> <gloss>the Moon/Presence</gloss> was seen in Israel, he was distressed and said, "I know that the Holy One, blessed be He, is angry with me, and because of me the Divine Presence did not descend upon Israel." And he said to Moses, "Moses my brother, is this how you have treated me? For I entered and I was put to shame." Immediately Moses entered with him, and they sought mercy, and the Divine Presence descended upon Israel (And he blessed them), and they went out from the tent. And after Aaron descended from the altar, Moses and Aaron went into the Tent of Meeting, for all that time they were standing and praying in the Tent of Meeting. And they went out and blessed the people. And these were, "May the pleasantness of the Lord our God be upon us," etc. And may it be His will.
</insert>

<insert></insert>
...upon it, that the Divine Presence would dwell in the work of your hands. For during all the seven days of the inauguration that Moses set up the Tabernacle, and served in it, and dismantled it every day, the Divine Presence did not dwell in it. And the Israelites were ashamed and said to Moses, "Moses our teacher, all the toil that we have toiled [was] so that the Divine Presence would dwell among us, and we would know that the sin of the golden calf was atoned for us." Therefore he said to them, "This is the thing which the Lord commanded that you should do; and the glory of the Lord shall appear to you." Aaron my brother is worthy and more esteemed than I, for through his offerings and his service the Divine Presence will dwell among you, and you will know that the Place <note>a rabbinic term for God</note> has chosen him. And therefore it is written in this section: "And fire went out from before the Lord." And Aaron said, "What... <note>The text remains fragmentary here</note>... Aaron sinned through me, and they strengthened the embers like Moses our teacher, and they heard them, for by the lives of the Lord... know that He, may He be blessed, said to him...

Priests, pray in the true words 
to God. Glory, Stephen, 
pray for us. Your prayer, a foundation, 
firm, for Stephen. Stephen, again, 
the faith, like Abraham, our father. 
Pure Stephen, full of grace and power, 
the bond of miracle, in the world. 
By the blessing of our Father, in the Highest, <gloss>Word of God</gloss>, and He said, one, 
to them, may mercy be ours, and glory befits. 
For them, the Holy Spirit, <gloss>Our Father</gloss>, 
Your aid, Stephen, glory as, three, 
the Holy Spirit, <gloss>with us all, Amen</gloss>. 
Stephen, martyr, praise the Holy 
Stephen, first martyr, father, pray 
for us, from the teachers. Your prayer, 
a foundation, may it reach us, <gloss>peace</gloss>. Stephen, 
righteous, of the first martyr, 
glory of God. And He said, I saw the 
heaven, opened, and the power, Son of God. 
Son, who sits at His right hand, <gloss>with</gloss>, two, 
Christ, peace, between them both, 
glory of mercy, between them. 
<gloss>Glory to God</gloss>, Stephen, pray, who 
encompasses the sky. And He said, forgive them, 
this sin, my transgression, <gloss>peace to the earth</gloss>. 
Faith, which does not shake. Stephen, 
pray for us. Your prayer, a 
foundation, may it reach us, <gloss>peace</gloss>. Stephen, 
righteous and good, preacher, the word of the Gospel, in 
all the earth, teacher. 
<gloss>Peace</gloss>, Holy Spirit, 
to Stephen. And He said, I saw the 
heavens, opened, and martyr, in all the world,

<header>العلم المذموم</header>

تمام الحول من وقت الإسلام ؛ فإن لم يملك إلا الإبل لم يلزمه إلا تعلم زكاة الإبل ، وكذلك في سائر الأصناف ، فإذا دخل في أشهر الحج فلا يلزمه المبادرة إلى علم الحج مع أن فعله على التراخي فلا يكون تعلمه على الفور ، ولكن ينبغي لعلماء الإسلام أن ينبهوه على أن الحج فرض على التراخي على كل من ملك الزاد والراحلة إذا كان هو مالكا حتى ربما يرى الحزم لنفسه في المبادرة فعند ذلك إذا عزم عليه لزمه تعلم كيفية الحج ولم يلزمه إلا تعلم أركانه وواجباته دون نوافله ، فإن فعل ذلك نفل فعله أيضاً نفل فلا يكون تعلمه فرض عين وفى تحريم السكوت عن التنبيه على وجوب أصل الحج فى الحال نظر يليق بالفقه ، وهكذا التدريج في علم سائر الأفعال التي هي فرض عين . وأما التروك فيجب تعلم علم ذلك بحسب ما يتجدد من الحال ، وذلك يختلف بحال الشخص إذ لا يجب على الأبكم تعلم ما يحرم من الكلام ، ولا على الأعمى تعلم ما يحرم من النظر ، ولا على البدوى تعلم ما يحرم الجلوس فيه من المساكن ، فذلك أيضاً واجب بحسب ما يقتضيه الحال ، فما يعلم أنه ينفك عنه لا يجب تعلمه وما هو ملابس له يجب تنبيهه عليه كما لو كان عند الإسلام لابساً للحرير ، أو جالساً في الغصب ، أو ناظراً إلى غير ذي محرم ، فيجب تعريفه بذلك وما ليس ملابساً له ولكنه بصدد التعرض له على القرب كالأكل والشرب فيجب تعليمه ، حتى إذا كان في بلد يتعاطى فيه شرب الخمر وأكل لحم الخنزير فيجب تعليمه ذلك وتنبيهه عليه ، وما وجب تعليمه وجب عليه تعلمه . وأما الاعتقادات وأعمال القلوب فيجب علمها بحسب الخواطر ، فإن خطر له شك في المعاني التي تدل عليها كلمتا الشهادة فيجب عليه تعلم ما يتوصل به إلى إزالة الشك . فإن لم يخطر له ذلك ومات قبل أن يعتقد أن كلام الله سبحانه قديم وأنه مرئى وأنه ليس محلا للحوادث إلى غير ذلك مما يذكر في المعتقدات ، فقد مات على الإسلام إجماعاً ، ولكن هذه الخواطر الموجبة للاعتقادات بعضها يخطر بالطبع وبعضها يخطر بالسماع من أهل البلد ، فإن كان في بلد شاع فيه الكلام وتناطق الناس بالبدع فينبغي أن يصان في أول بلوغه عنها بتلقين الحق ، فإنه لو ألقى إليه الباطل لوجبت إزالته عن قلبه وربما عسر ذلك ، كما أنه لو كان هذا المسلم تاجراً وقد شاع في البلد معاملة الربا وجب عليه تعلم الحذر من الربا ، وهذا هو الحق في العلم الذي هو فرض عين ومعناه العلم بكيفية العمل الواجب ، فمن علم العلم الواجب ووقت وجوبه فقد علم العلم الذي هو فرض عين ، وما ذكره الصوفية من فهم خواطر العدو ولمة الملك حق أيضاً ولكن في حق من يتصدى له ، فإذا كان الغالب أن الإنسان لا ينفك عن دواعى الشر والرياء والحسد فيلزمه أن يتعلم من علم ربع المهلكات ما يرى نفسه محتاجاً إليه ، وكيف لا يجب عليه وقد قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم « ثلاث مهلكات : شح مطاع ، وهوى متبع ، وإعجاب المرء بنفسه » (١) ولا ينفك عنها بشر ، وبقية ما سنذكره من مذمومات أحوال القلب كالكبر والعجب وأخواتها تتبع هذه الثلاث المهلكات ، وإزالتها فرض عين ، ولا يمكن إزالتها إلا بمعرفة حدودها ومعرفة أسبابها ومعرفة علاماتها ومعرفة علاجها ؛ فإن من لا يعرف الشر يقع فيه ، والعلاج هو مقابلة السبب بضده ، وكيف يمكن دون معرفة السبب والمسبب ، وأكثر ما ذكرناه في ربع المهلكات من فروض الأعيان ، وقد تركها الناس كافة اشتغالا بما لا يعنى . ومما ينبغى أن يبادر في إلقائه إليه إذا لم يكن قد انتقل من ملة إلى ملة أخرى : الإيمان بالجنة والنار والحشر والنشر حتى يؤمن به ويصدق ، وهو من تتمة كلمتي الشهادة ، فإنه بعد التصديق بكونه عليه السلام رسولا

---

(١) حديث ( ثلاث مهلكات : شح مطاع ... الحديث ) أخرجه البزار والطبراني وأبو نعيم والبيهقي في الشعب من حديث أنس بإسناد ضعيف

<header>Blameworthy Knowledge</header>

the completion of the year from the time of becoming Muslim. If he possesses only camels, he is only obligated to learn the alms for camels, and likewise for other types of assets. If he enters the months of Hajj, he is not obligated to rush to learn the rules of Hajj, as the action itself is delayed <note>meaning: it does not have to be performed the moment one is obligated</note>, so learning it is not immediate. However, it is appropriate for the scholars of Islam to alert him that Hajj is an obligation upon everyone who possesses the provisions and the mount, if he is the owner, so that he may see the prudence in rushing to do it. Upon that, if he resolves to perform it, it becomes obligatory for him to learn the method of Hajj, but he is not obligated except to learn its pillars and requirements, not its supererogatory acts. If he performs them, they are voluntary, and learning them is not an individual obligation. There is a legal consideration regarding the prohibition of remaining silent about alerting one to the obligation of Hajj in the present time. This is how the gradation works for the knowledge of all other actions that are individual obligations. As for the abstentions, one must learn the knowledge of them according to the circumstances that arise, which vary according to the person. It is not obligatory for a mute person to learn what is prohibited in speech, nor for a blind person to learn what is prohibited in looking, nor for a Bedouin to learn the prohibitions regarding sitting in certain types of buildings. These are also obligatory according to the demands of the situation. Whatever one is known to be removed from, learning it is not obligatory, but whatever one is involved in, one must be alerted to it. As if, upon becoming Muslim, he were wearing silk, or sitting on usurped property, or looking at someone not within the forbidden degree of marriage, he must be informed of that. Whatever he is not involved in, but is likely to face soon—such as eating and drinking—must be taught to him. If he is in a city where drinking wine and eating pork are common, he must be taught about that and alerted to it, and whatever is obligatory to be taught, it is obligatory for him to learn. As for beliefs and the actions of the heart, they must be known according to the occurrences of one's thoughts. If a doubt occurs to him regarding the meanings indicated by the two words of testimony, he must learn what is needed to remove that doubt. If that does not occur to him, and he dies before believing that the speech of God the Exalted is eternal, and that He is visible, and that He is not a location for temporal events, and other things mentioned in the articles of faith, he has died a Muslim by consensus. However, some of these thoughts that necessitate beliefs occur by nature, and some occur through hearing from the people of the land. If he is in a land where theological debate is widespread and people speak of innovations, he should be protected at the start of his puberty from them by being taught the truth. If falsehood is cast upon him, it would be obligatory to remove it from his heart, though that might be difficult. Just as if this Muslim were a merchant and usury <term>riba</term> <gloss>usury/interest</gloss> was common in the land, it would be obligatory for him to learn how to avoid it. This is the truth concerning the knowledge that is an individual obligation, and its meaning is knowledge of the method of the obligatory action. Whoever knows the obligatory knowledge and the time of its obligation has known the knowledge that is an individual obligation. What the Sufis mentioned about understanding the whisperings of the enemy and the angel is also true, but for the one who attends to that. If it is the case that a person is not free from the motives of evil, hypocrisy, and envy, then it is incumbent upon him to learn from the quarter of "Destructive Things" what he sees himself in need of. How could it not be obligatory upon him, when the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "Three things are destructive: avarice that is obeyed, desires that are followed, and a person's vanity regarding himself." No human is free from these. The rest of what we will mention regarding the blameworthy states of the heart, such as pride, vanity, and their sisters, follow these three destructive things, and removing them is an individual obligation. It is impossible to remove them except by knowing their limits, their causes, their signs, and their cures. For one who does not know evil falls into it. The cure is to counter the cause with its opposite, and how can that be possible without knowing the cause and the effect? Most of what we mentioned in the quarter of "Destructive Things" is among the individual obligations, yet all the people have neglected them, occupying themselves with what does not concern them. Among the things one should hasten to present to him, if he has not transferred from one religion to another, is the belief in Paradise, Hell, the Resurrection, and the Gathering, so that he may believe in them and affirm them. This is part of the completion of the two words of testimony, for after affirming that he, peace be upon him, is a messenger...

---

(1) The hadith "Three things are destructive..." was narrated by al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* from Anas with a weak chain of narration.

<header>وظائف المرشد المعلم</header>

الدنيا على قصد الآخرة لا على قصد الدنيا ، وأما التعليم على قصد الدنيا فهو هلاك وإهلاك نعوذ بالله منه . وكما أن حق أبناء الرجل الواحد أن يتحابوا ويتعاونوا على المقاصد كلها فكذلك حق تلامذة الرجل الواحد التحاب والتوادد ولا يكون إلا كذلك إن كان مقصدهم الآخرة ولا يكون إلا التحاسد والتباغض إن كان مقصدهم الدنيا . فإن العلماء وأبناء الآخرة مسافرون إلى الله تعالى وسالكون إليه الطريق من الدنيا ، وسنوها وشهورها منازل الطريق . والترافق في الطريق بين المسافرين إلى الأمصار سبب التواد والتحاب فكيف السفر إلى الفردوس الأعلى والترافق في طريقه ؟ ولا ضيق في سعادة الآخرة فلذلك لا يكون بين أبناء الآخرة تنازع ولا سعة في سعادات الدنيا فلذلك لا ينفك عن ضيق التزاحم . والعدلون إلى طلب الرياسة بالعلوم خارجون عن موجب قوله تعالى ( إنما المؤمنون إخوة ) وداخلون في مقتضى قوله تعالى ( الأخلاء يومئذ بعضهم لبعض عدو إلا المتقين ) ( الوظيفة الثانية ) أن يقتدى لصاحب الشرع صلوات الله عليه وسلامه فلا يطلب على إفادة العلم أجرا ولا يقصد به جزاء ولا شكراً بل يعلم لوجه الله تعالى وطلبا للتقرب إليه ولا يرى لنفسه منة عليهم وإن كانت المنة لازمة عليهم بل يرى الفضل لهم إذ هذبوا قلوبهم لأن تتقرب إلى الله تعالى بزراعة العلوم فيها ، كالذي يعيرك الأرض لتزرع فيها لنفسك زراعة فمنفعتك بها تزيد على منفعة صاحب الأرض فكيف تقلده منة وثوابك في التعليم أكثر من ثواب المتعلم عند الله تعالى ؟ ولولا المتعلم ما نلت هذا الثواب فلا تطلب الأجر إلا من الله تعالى كما قال عز وجل ( ويا قوم لا أسألكم عليه مالا إن أجري إلا على الله ) فإن المال وما في الدنيا خادم البدن والبدن مركب النفس ومطيتها والمخدوم هو العلم إذ به شرف النفس . فمن طلب بالعلم المال كان كمن مسح أسفل مداسه بوجهه لينظفه فجعل المخدوم خادما والخادم مخدوما وذلك هو الانتكاس على أم الرأس ، ومثله هو الذي يقوم في العرض الأكبر مع المجرمين ناكسي رءوسهم عند ربهم . وعلى الجملة فالفضل والمنة للمعلم فانظر كيف انتهى أمر الدين إلى قوم يزعمون أن مقصودهم التقرب إلى الله تعالى بما هم فيه من علم الفقه والكلام والتدريس فيهما وفي غيرهما ؟ فانهم يبذلون المال والجاه ويتحملون أصناف الذل في خدمة السلاطين لاستطلاق الجرايات ولو تركوا ذلك لتركوا ولم يختلف إليهم ثم يتوقع المعلم من المتعلم أن يقوم له في كل نائبة وينصر وليه ويعادي عدوه وينتهض جهارا له في حاجاته ومسخرا بين يديه في أوطاره : فإن قصر في حقه ثار عليه وصار من أعدى أعدائه . فأخسس لعالم يرضى لنفسه بهذه المنزلة ثم يفرح بها ثم لا يستحي من أن يقول غرضي من التدريس نشر العلم تقربا إلى الله تعالى ونصرة لدينه ! فانظر إلى الأمارات حتى ترى ضروب الاغترارات ( الوظيفه الثالثة ) أن لا يدع من نصح المتعلم شيئا وذلك بأن يمنعه من التصدي لرتبة قبل استحقاقها والتشاغل بعلم خفي قبل الفراغ من الجلي ثم ينبهه على أن الغرض بطلب العلوم القرب إلى الله تعالى دون الرياسة والمباهاة والمنافسة ، ويقدم تقبيح ذلك في نفسه بأقصى ما يمكن فليس ما يصلحه العالم الفاجر بأكثر مما يفسده : فإن علم من باطنه أنه لا يطلب العلم إلا للدنيا نظر إلى العلم الذي يطلبه فإن كان هو علم الخلاف في الفقه والجدل في الكلام والفتاوى في الخصومات والأحكام فيمنعه من ذلك فإن هذه العلوم ليست من علوم الآخرة ولا من العلوم التي قيل فيها " تعلمنا العلم لغير الله فأبى العلم أن يكون إلا لله " ، وإنما ذلك علم التفسير وعلم الحديث وما كان الأولون يشتغلون به من علم الآخرة ومعرفة أخلاق النفس وكيفية تهذيبها فإذا تعلمه الطالب وقصد به الدنيا فلا بأس أن يتركه فإنه يثمر له طمعا في الوعظ والاستتباع ولكن قد ينتبه في أثناء الأمر أو آخره إذ فيه العلوم المخوفة من الله تعالى المحقرة للدنيا المعظمة للآخرة ، وذلك

...the world with the intention of the Hereafter, not with the intention of this world. As for teaching with a worldly intention, it is destruction and the causing of destruction; we seek refuge in God from it. 

Just as it is the right of a man's biological sons to love one another and cooperate in all goals, it is likewise the right of a single teacher's students to love and cherish one another. This will only happen if their goal is the Hereafter; if their goal is this world, there will be nothing but envy and hatred. This is because scholars and the children of the Hereafter are travelers toward God the Almighty, journeying to Him from this world. Its years and months are the stations of the path. Traveling together on the road to worldly cities is a cause for love and affection, so how much more so for the journey to the Highest Paradise? 

There is no crowding in the happiness of the Hereafter, so there is no dispute among its children. However, there is no room in the happiness of this world, so it is never free from the pressure of competition. Those who turn toward seeking leadership through the sciences have departed from the requirement of God's saying: {The believers are but brothers} <note>Qur'an 49:10</note> and have entered into the implication of His saying: {Friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except for the righteous} <note>Qur'an 43:67</note>.

**The Second Duty:** To follow the example of the Lawgiver <note>the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him</note>. He should not seek a fee for providing knowledge, nor seek a reward or even gratitude. Rather, he should teach for the sake of God the Almighty and to seek proximity to Him. He should not feel that he has bestowed a favor upon the students, even though a favor is owed to him by them. Instead, he should see the merit as belonging to them, as they have refined their hearts to draw closer to God by planting knowledge within them. This is like someone who lends you land so you may plant for yourself; your benefit from it is greater than the benefit of the landowner. How then can you claim a favor over them when your reward in teaching is greater than the student's reward before God? Were it not for the student, you would not have attained this reward. Do not seek payment except from God the Almighty, as He said: {O my people, I ask of you no wealth for it. My reward is only from God} <note>Qur'an 11:29</note>. 

Wealth and the things of this world are the servants of the body, and the body is the vessel and mount of the soul. The thing to be served is knowledge, as through it the soul gains nobility. Whoever seeks wealth through knowledge is like one who wipes the bottom of his shoe with his face to clean it; he has made the served into a servant and the servant into the served. This is an inversion of priorities. Such a person is like those who will stand in the Great Gathering with the criminals, their heads hanging low before their Lord. 

In summary, the merit and the favor belong to the teacher. Look at how the state of religion has fallen to people who claim that their intention is to draw closer to God through their study of jurisprudence and theology, and their teaching of these and other subjects! They spend wealth and status and endure all types of humiliation in the service of rulers to obtain salaries. If they left that, they would be left alone, and no one would visit them. Then, the teacher expects the student to stand by him in every calamity, to support his ally, to oppose his enemy, to rise up openly for his needs, and to be enslaved before him for his desires. If the student falls short in his right, the teacher turns against him and becomes one of his fiercest enemies. How vile is a scholar who accepts this position for himself, then rejoices in it, then is not ashamed to say "My purpose in teaching is to spread knowledge to draw closer to God and to support His religion!" Look at the signs until you see the various forms of delusion.

**The Third Duty:** That he should not withhold any advice from the student. This is by preventing the student from aspiring to a rank before he is worthy of it, or occupying himself with a hidden science before finishing the clear ones. Then, he should alert him that the purpose of seeking knowledge is closeness to God the Almighty, not leadership, boasting, or competition. He should present the ugliness of such goals in the student's soul as much as possible. For what a corrupt scholar rectifies is not more than what he ruins. 

If the teacher knows from the student's inner self that he seeks knowledge only for the world, he should look at the science the student is seeking. If it is the science of legal disputation, dialectical theology, or legal opinions for lawsuits and judgments, he should prevent him from that. For these sciences are not from the sciences of the Hereafter, nor from the sciences of which it was said, "We learned knowledge for other than God, but the knowledge refused to be for anyone but God." That quote refers to the science of <term>Tafsir</term> <gloss>Qur'anic interpretation</gloss>, the science of <term>Hadith</term> <gloss>Prophetic traditions</gloss>, and what the predecessors occupied themselves with regarding the science of the Hereafter and knowing the character of the soul and how to refine it. If the student learns that while intending the world, there is no harm in leaving him to it, for it will produce in him a desire for preaching and gaining a following, but he may wake up during the process or at the end of it, for it contains the sciences that inspire fear of God, belittle the world, and magnify the Hereafter. This text is from the **Brihadaranyaka Upanishad**, one of the oldest and most important Upanishads, specifically from the **Kanva Recension, Fourth Adhyaya, Fourth Brahmana (Verses 7-10)**. It discusses the nature of liberation (*moksha*), the state of the realized soul, and the paths of knowledge vs. ignorance.

### Verse 7
**Sanskrit:** यदा सर्वे प्रमुच्यन्ते कामा येऽस्य हृदि श्रिताः । अथ मर्त्योऽमृतो भवत्यत्र ब्रह्म समश्नुत इति ॥ ७ ॥
**Transliteration:** *yadā sarve pramucyante kāmā ye'sya hṛdi śritāḥ | atha martyo'mṛto bhavatyatra brahma samaśnuta iti || 7 ||*
**Translation:** When all desires that dwell in the heart are cast off, then the mortal becomes immortal and attains <term>Brahman</term> <gloss>the Absolute</gloss> here.

**Breakdown:**
*   **yadā**: when
*   **sarve**: all
*   **pramucyante**: are cast off / liberated / abandoned
*   **kāmā**: desires
*   **ye'sya**: which [are] of him
*   **hṛdi**: in the heart
*   **śritāḥ**: residing / dwelling
*   **atha**: then
*   **martyaḥ**: mortal (man)
*   **amṛtaḥ**: immortal
*   **bhavati**: becomes
*   **atra**: here (in this body/life)
*   **brahma**: <term>Brahman</term> <gloss>the Supreme Reality</gloss>
*   **samaśnute**: attains / enjoys / realizes
*   **iti**: (ends the quote)

---

### Verse 7 (continued)
**Sanskrit:* तद्यथाऽहिनिर्व्लयनी वल्मीके मृता प्रत्यस्ता शयीत, एवमेवेदं शरीरं शेते ।
**Transliteration:** *tad yathā-ahirvlayanī valmīke mṛtā pratyastā śayīta, evam evedaṃ śarīraṃ śete |*
**Translation:** Just as the slough of a snake lies dead and cast off on an anthill, so too does this body lie.

**Breakdown:**
*   **tad yathā**: just as / for example
*   **ahi-vlayanī**: the slough/skin of a snake
*   **valmīke**: on an anthill
*   **mṛtā**: dead
*   **pratyastā**: cast off / thrown away
*   **śayīta**: lies
*   **evam eva**: even so / in the very same way
*   **idaṃ**: this
*   **śarīraṃ**: body
*   **śete**: lies

---

### Verse 7 (continued)
**Sanskrit:** अथायमशरीरोऽमृतः प्राणो ब्रह्मैव तेज एव । ‘सोऽहं भगवते सहस्रं ददामि’ इति होवाca जनको वैदेहः ॥ ७ ॥
**Transliteration:** *athāyam-aśarīro-'mṛtaḥ prāṇo brahmaiva teja eva | 'so'haṃ bhagavate sahasraṃ dadāmi' iti hovāca janako vaidehaḥ || 7 ||*
**Translation:** Then this disembodied, immortal life is <term>Brahman</term> <gloss>the Absolute</gloss> alone, it is light alone. "I will give you a thousand [cows], Lord," said King Janaka, king of the Videhas.

**Breakdown:**
*   **atha**: now / then
*   **ayam**: this
*   **aśarīraḥ**: disembodied / bodiless
*   **amṛtaḥ**: immortal
*   **prāṇaḥ**: life / life-force / vital breath
*   **brahma eva**: <term>Brahman</term> <gloss>the Supreme</gloss> indeed
*   **teja eva**: light / splendor indeed
*   **so'haṃ** (saḥ aham): I
*   **bhagavate**: to the Worshipful One / Lord (referring to the sage Yajnavalkya)
*   **sahasraṃ**: a thousand (usually referring to cows)
*   **dadāmi**: I give
*   **iti ha uvāca**: thus said
*   **janako vaidehaḥ**: Janaka, King of Videha

---

### Verse 8
**Sanskrit:** अणुः पन्था विततः पुराणो मां स्पृष्टोऽनुवित्तो मयैव । तेन धीरा अपियन्ति ब्रह्मविदः स्वर्गं लोकमित ऊर्ध्वं विमुक्ताः ॥ ८ ॥
**Transliteration:** *aṇuḥ panthā vitataḥ purāṇo māṃ spṛṣṭo'nuvitto mayaiva | tena dhīrā apiyanti brahmavidaḥ svargaṃ lokam-ita ūrdhvaṃ vmuuktāḥ || 8 ||*
**Translation:** The ancient path is fine, vast, and stretched out. It has been touched and found by me alone. By it, the wise, the knowers of <term>Brahman</term> <gloss>the Absolute</gloss>, ascend to the heavenly world, liberated from here upward.

**Breakdown:**
*   **aṇuḥ**: subtle / fine
*   **panthā**: path
*   **vitataḥ**: spread out / extended
*   **purāṇaḥ**: ancient / old
*   **mām**: me
*   **spṛṣṭaḥ**: touched / reached
*   **anuvittaḥ**: found / discovered / realized
*   **mayā eva**: by me alone
*   **tena**: by that (path)
*   **dhīrāḥ**: the wise / the steady-minded
*   **apiyanti**: go / attain / reach
*   **brahmavidaḥ**: knowers of <term>Brahman</term>
*   **svargaṃ lokam**: heavenly world / world of light (here meaning liberation)
*   **itaḥ**: from here
*   **ūrdhvam**: upward / above
*   **vimuktāḥ**: liberated / released

---

### Verse 9
**Sanskrit:** तस्मिञ्छुक्लममुत नीलमाहुः पिङ्गलं हरितं लोहितं च । एष पन्था ब्रह्मणा हानुवित्तस्तेनैति ब्रह्मवित्पुण्यकृत्तैजसश्च ॥ ९ ॥
**Transliteration:** *tasmiñ chuklam-uta nīlam-āhuḥ piṅgalaṃ haritaṃ lohitaṃ ca | eṣa panthā brahmaṇā hānuvittas-tenaiti brahmavit-puṇyakṛt-taijasaśca || 9 ||*
**Translation:** They speak of white, blue, tawny, green, and red in it. This path is found by <term>Brahman</term> <gloss>the Absolute</gloss>. By it, the knower of <term>Brahman</term> <gloss>the Absolute</gloss>, the doer of good, and the radiant one proceeds.

**Breakdown:**
*   **tasmin**: in that / upon it
*   **śuklam**: white
*   **uta**: also / and
*   **nīlam**: blue
*   **āhuḥ**: they say
*   **piṅgalaṃ**: tawny / brown / golden
*   **haritaṃ**: green
*   **lohitaṃ**: red
*   **ca**: and
*   **eṣa**: this
*   **panthā**: path
*   **brahmaṇā**: by <term>Brahman</term>
*   **ha**: indeed
*   **anuvittaḥ**: found / attained
*   **tena**: by it
*   **eti**: goes / travels
*   **brahmavit**: knower of <term>Brahman</term>
*   **puṇyakṛt**: doer of good / virtuous
*   **taijasaḥ**: radiant / full of light

---

### Verse 10
**Sanskrit:** अन्धं तमः प्रविशन्ति येऽविद्यामुपासते । ततो भूय इव ते तमो य उ विद्यायां रताः ॥ १० ॥
**Transliteration:** *andhaṃ tamaḥ praviśanti ye'vidyām-upāsate | tato bhūya iva te tamo ya u vidyāyāṃ ratāḥ || 10 ||*
**Translation:** Into blind darkness they enter who worship <term>avidyā</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss>. Into even greater darkness do they enter who are content with <term>vidyā</term> <gloss>knowledge</gloss>.

**Breakdown:**
*   **andham**: blind
*   **tamaḥ**: darkness
*   **praviśanti**: enter
*   **ye**: those who
*   **avidyām**: ignorance (often refers to ritualistic action without knowledge)
*   **upāsate**: worship / devote themselves to
*   **tataḥ**: than that
*   **bhūya**: greater / more
*   **iva**: as if / even
*   **te**: those
*   **tamas**: darkness
*   **ya u**: who indeed
*   **vidyāyām**: in knowledge (often refers to intellectual knowledge without realization)
*   **ratāḥ**: delighted / absorbed / devoted

***

<summary>
These verses from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad describe the state of liberation where the soul, freed from desire, realizes its identity with Brahman. They also warn against the lopsided pursuit of either mere ritual (avidya) or mere intellectual knowledge (vidya) without true realization.
</summary>

# CH. I. THE TITLE STROMATEIS.

the *Hypotyposes* and the *Quis Dives Salvetur* preceded the *Miscellanies*. The former, and possibly the latter, may be referred to in the promised discussion *On Prophecy*. Granting that it was at one time Clement's intention to bring out a complete treatise on Christian Gnosis under the name *Didaskalos*, I do not see why the same reasons which led him to prepare the way for this by the *Stromateis* should not also have suggested to him to bring out his great work in portions.

We have still to answer the question, what were the reasons which induced Clement to follow up the *Paedagogus* by a work, of which the real character was disguised by its apparent disorder? Perhaps the following quotation from De Faye's preface may help to clear the ground.

"What makes the century of Clement of Alexandria so interesting is that it is, like our own, an epoch of transition where the fertile seeds of the future are fermenting. It is an undecided and troubled hour, where the beliefs and institutions of the following centuries are being prepared. Clement himself and his work cannot leave us indifferent. He was essentially a man of transition. Before him, Christianity still has something primitive; in many respects the new faith had not passed the embryonic state. After him, it is a constituted religion. A prodigious transformation is taking place within the Church toward the end of the second century. Clement was one of its most powerful laborers. He is the true creator of ecclesiastical theology. What a path covered by Christian thought from the Apostolic Fathers to Origen! It is Clement who is the responsible author of this astonishing evolution. It is for this reason that he occupies a place of the first order in the history of Christian ideas."

The early Christians for the most part looked upon the Greco-Roman literature as a part of the hostile world against which they were warned. It was necessity which compelled the Apologists, such as Quadratus and Aristides, to enter this new domain in the reign of Hadrian. The Third. God, you who are the truth, and you love the truth,
guide us in the way of your truth,
and make us worthy that we may draw near to you in purity,
and fast a fast that is pleasing to you,
and be cleansed from all the defilements of sin,
and serve you in fear,
and in righteousness all the days of our lives. And make us worthy that with joy
and with gladness we may reach the day of your glorious resurrection,
and there we shall praise you with all your saints,
our Lord and our God unto the ages.
Amen. Deacon: Let us stand well. Priest: God, who are the pardoner of sinners,
and the forgiver of faults, and merciful
to all the penitents, you, my Lord, in your great mercies,
have mercy on us all, and make us worthy that we may draw near
to you in purity, and fast a fast that is pleasing to you,
and be cleansed from all the defilements of sin,
and make us worthy that with joy and with gladness we may reach the day
of your glorious resurrection, and there we shall praise you with all your saints,
our Lord and our God unto the ages. Amen. Deacon: Let us stand well.

**Top Panel**

འབྱིན་པའོ། །མི་གདུང་བའི་ལྟ་བའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་བྱིན་པའོ། །འདོད་མཛད་པའི་ལྟ་བའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་བྱིན་པའོ། །རྒྱ་ཆེན་མཐོང་བའི་ལྟ་བའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་བྱིན་པའོ། །འཇམ་མཐོང་བའི་ལྟ་བའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་བྱིན་པའོ། །རྣམ་གསལ་མཐོང་བའི་ལྟ་བའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་བྱིན་པའོ། །བྱང་ཟང་མེད་པའི་ལྟ་བའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་བྱིན་པའོ། །འཇུག་པས་མེད་པའི་ལྟ་བའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་བྱིན་པའོ། །རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་བྱིན་པའོ། །ལན་ཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོང་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་བྱིན་པའོ། །ཕྱིར་མི་འོང་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་བྱིན་པའོ། །དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉིད་བྱིན་པའོ། །ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་བྱིན་པའོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་། །དེ་བཞིན་ལྟ་བའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་གྱི་ལམ་རྣམ་པར་བསྟན་ཏེ། །དེ་བས་བསླབ་པས་ལམ་གསལ་མོ་ཞིང་མཐོ་བ་རྣམས་ཡོད་དོ། །བྲམ་ཟེའི་རིགས་མེད་པའི་མཐོ་བ་རྣམས་ཡོད་དོ། །ཁྱིམ་བདག་གི་རིགས་མེད་པའི་མཐོ་བ་རྣམས་ཡོད་དོ། །རྒྱལ་ཆེན་བཞིའི་རིགས་ཀྱི་ལྷ་རྣམས་

གྱི་ལྷ་རྣམས་ཡོད་དོ། །འདུན་ཤེས་མེད་པའི་ལྟ་བའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་རྣམས་ཡོད་དོ། །རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡོད་དོ། །ལན་ཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོང་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡོད་དོ། །ཕྱིར་མི་འོང་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡོད་དོ། །དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉིད་ཡོད་དོ། །རྣམ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཡིད་རྟེན་ཡོད་དོ། །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ལམ་དུ་བྱིན་པ་འདི་ཡོད་དོ། །བསམ་གཏན་ནི་ཡོད་དོ། །ཚད་མེད་པ་ནི་ཡོད་དོ། །གཟུགས་མེད་པའི་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་ནི་ཡོད་དོ། །དྲན་པ་ཉེར་བཞག་རྣམས་ནི་ཡོད་དོ། །ཡང་དག་པར་སྤོང་བ་ནི་ཡོད་དོ། །རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་རྐང་པ་ནི་ཡོད་དོ། །དབང་པོ་ལྔ་ཡོད་དོ། །སྟོབས་ལྔ་ཡོད་དོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་རྣམས་ཡོད་དོ། །འཕགས་པའི་ལམ་ཡན་ལག་བརྒྱད་པ་ཡོད་དོ། །སྒོམ་པའི་ལམ་དུ་བྱིན་པ་ཡོད་དོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ལམ་དུ་བྱིན་པ་ཡོད་དོ། །བཟོད་པའི་ལམ་དུ་བྱིན་པ་ཡོད་དོ། །བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱི་ལམ་དུ་བྱིན་པ་ཡོད་དོ། །བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ལམ་དུ་བྱིན་པ་ཡོད་དོ། །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ལམ་དུ་བྱིན་པ་ཡོད་དོ། །མཐོང་བ་ཉིད་ཡོད་དོ། །སྤོང་བ་ཉིད་ཡོད་དོ། །སྒོམ་པ་ཉིད་ཡོད་དོ། །སྤོང་བ་

The limbs of enlightenment exist. The eightfold noble path exists. The path of meditation is present. The path of discipline is present. The path of patience is present. The path of diligence is present. The path of meditative stabilization is present. The path of wisdom is present. The seeing itself exists. The abandoning itself exists. The meditation itself exists. Abandoning.

二月十日にのりてふふみや
えにふみあつめふてん
乃くのまんごーとぶ
ゆんのらんせさうの
うきさうざしおし
あひつるのよめ
とぞおもひてす
ひめみやうらやまし
さねさくのられる
けふはあやうく
ーのいづくこうらむ

<column-break/>

とふりいふささん
かくるーらるるゆめ
がれーやんる
ひめれはつんひょん
てんふんのやうが
てうわひうざるる
どのゆふひーと
ひつりのあはれち
あひよあひてちう
うどのあやうい
はひめさへひり
ぬふゆーび
くるやてわ

みちのくの国に、文正といふ長者あり。
この長者、子なくして、日夜神仏に祈りけるに、
やがて懐妊して、男子を産みたり。
その名を文正とぞ名付けける。
この文正、成長して、いと美しき男になりにけり。
心もやさしく、情け深き人にて、
世の人、皆あやしびけり。

それより、この国の
とこの山に、ひゃうしんといふ
みかどおはして、おほいに
おどろき給ふ。

かくて、みかど
つひに、おほやけに
あらはれ給ふ。

よのふしぎなる人よ
らちもなきことなり
はかりごとあり。

<meta>continues from the previous page: the text transitions from the repetitive description of a nun walking to the beginning of the story of Bunshō in the province of Michinoku.</meta>

In the province of <term>Michinoku</term> <gloss>the northern region of Japan, also known as Mutsu</gloss>, there was a <term>chōja</term> <gloss>a person of great wealth and local influence</gloss> named <term>Bunshō</term>.
This wealthy man had no children. He prayed to the gods and Buddhas day and night.
Before long, his wife conceived and gave birth to a boy.
He was given the name Bunshō.
As this Bunshō grew, he became an exceptionally beautiful man.
He had a gentle heart and was a person of deep compassion.
All the people in the world found him remarkable <note>original: "ayashibiki," meaning to find someone strange, miraculous, or extraordinary</note>.

From that time, in <term>Mount Toko</term> of this province,
a <term>mikado</term> <gloss>emperor or sovereign ruler</gloss> named <term>Hyōshin</term> <gloss>a name or title; likely a corruption of "Hyōe-no-shin"</gloss> resided.
He was greatly surprised by these events.

Thus, the <term>mikado</term>
finally appeared
in public.

"What a strange person in this world!
This is an absurd matter.
There is some plot involved."

<summary>This page introduces the protagonist Bunshō, a miraculous and handsome child born to a wealthy man in northern Japan after fervent prayers. A local ruler named Hyōshin takes notice of Bunshō's extraordinary nature with suspicion and surprise.</summary>
<keywords>Bunshō, Michinoku, chōja, Hyōshin, miraculous birth, Mount Toko</keywords>

καὶ τιμῆς ἂν εἴη τοιῶνδε περὶ τὰς ἡδονὰς καλουμένας, οἷον σιτίων τε καὶ ποτῶν; ἥκιστα ἔφη ὁ Σιμμίας. τί δὲ τῶν ἀφροδισίων; οὐδαμῶς.
τί δὲ τὰς ἄλλας τὰς περὶ τὸ σῶμα θεραπείας; οἴει ἐντίμους εἶναι τῷ τοιούτῳ; οἷον ἱματίων διαφερόντων κτήσεις καὶ ὑποδημάτων καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους
καλλωπισμοὺς τοὺς περὶ τὸ σῶμα, πότερον τιμᾶν δοκεῖ σοι ἢ ἀτιμάζειν, καθ᾽ ὅσον μὴ πολλὴ ἀνάγκη μετέχειν αὐτῶν; ἀτιμάζειν ἔμοιγε δοκεῖ, ἔφη,
ὅ γε ὡς ἀληθῶς φιλόσοφος. οὐκοῦν ὅλως δοκεῖ σοι, ἔφη, ἡ τοῦ τοιούτου πραγματεία
οὐ περὶ τὸ σῶμα εἶναι, ἀλλὰ καθ᾽ ὅσον δύναται ἀφεστάναι αὐτοῦ, πρὸς δὲ τὴν ψυχὴν τετράφθαι; ἔμοιγε. ἆρ᾽ οὖν πρῶτον
ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις δῆλός ἐστιν ὁ φιλόσοφος ἀπολύων ὅτι μάλιστα τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπὸ τῆς τοῦ σώματος κοινωνίας διαφερόντως τῶν
ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων; φαίνεται. καὶ δοκεῖ γέ που, ὦ Σιμμία, τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀνθρώποις ᾧ μηδὲν ἡδὺ τῶν τοιούτων μηδὲ μετέχει αὐτῶν,
οὐκ ἄξιον εἶναι ζῆν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐγγύς τι τείνειν τοῦ τεθνάναι ὁ μηδὲν φροντίζων τῶν ἡδονῶν αἳ διὰ τοῦ σώματός εἰσιν. πάνυ μὲν
ἀληθῆ λέγεις. τί δὲ δὴ περὶ αὐτὴν τὴν τῆς φρονήσεως κτῆσιν; πότερον ἐμπόδιον τὸ σῶμα ἢ οὔ, ἐάν τις αὐτὸ ἐν τῇ ζητήσει
κοινωνὸν συμπαραλαμβάνῃ; οἷον τὸ τοιόνδε λέγω· ἆρα ἔχει ἀλήθειάν τινα ὄψις τε καὶ ἀκοὴ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, ἢ τά γε τοιαῦτα
καὶ οἱ ποιηταὶ ἡμῖν ἀεὶ θρυλοῦσιν, ὅτι οὔτ᾽ ἀκούομεν ἀκριβὲς οὐδὲν οὔτε ὁρῶμεν; καίτοι εἰ αὗται τῶν περὶ τὸ σῶμα αἰσθήσεων
μὴ ἀκριβεῖς εἰσι μηδὲ σαφεῖς, σχολῇ αἵ γε ἄλλαι· πᾶσαι γάρ που τούτων φαῦλότεραί εἰσιν. ἢ σοὶ οὐ δοκοῦσιν; πάνυ μὲν

ἐξαπατᾶται ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ. ἀληθῆ λέγεις. ἆρ᾽ οὖν οὐκ ἐν τῷ λογίζεσθαι εἴπερ που ἄλλοθι κατάδηλον αὐτῇ γίγνεταί τι τῶν

λύπη μήτε τις ἡδονή, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι μάλιστα αὐτὴ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν γίγνηται ἐῶσα χαίρειν τὸ σῶμα, καὶ καθ᾽ ὅσον δύναται
μηδὲ κοινωνοῦσα αὐτῷ μηδ᾽ ἁπτομένη ὀρέγηται τοῦ ὄντος. ἔστι ταῦτα. οὐκοῦν καὶ ἐνταῦθα ἡ τοῦ φιλοσόφου ψυχὴ
μάλιστα ἀτιμάζει τὸ σῶμα καὶ φεύγει ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, ζητεῖ δὲ αὐτὴ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν γίγνεσθαι; φαίνεται. τί δὲ δὴ τὰ τοιάδε, ὦ
Σιμμία; φαμέν τι εἶναι δίκαιον αὐτὸ ἢ οὐδέν; φαμὲν μέντοι νὴ Δία. καὶ καλόν γέ τι καὶ ἀγαθόν; πῶς δ᾽ οὔ;

διὰ τοῦ σώματος ἐφήψω αὐτῶν; λέγω δὲ περὶ πάντων, οἷον μεγέθους πέρι, ὑγιείας, ἰσχύος, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἑνὶ λόγῳ ἁπάντων
τῆς οὐσίας ὃ τυγχάνει ἕκαστον ὄν· ἆρα διὰ τοῦ σώματος αὐτῶν τὸ ἀληθέστατον θεωρεῖται, ἢ ὧδε ἔχει· ὃς ἂν μάλιστα
ἡμῶν καὶ ἀκριβέστατα παρασκευάσηται αὐτὸ ἕκαστον διανοηθῆναι περὶ οὗ σκοπεῖ, οὗτος ἂν ἐγγύτατα ἴοι τοῦ γνῶναι ἕκαστον;
πάνυ μὲν οὖν. ἆρ᾽ οὖν ἐκεῖνος ἂν τοῦτο ποιήσειε καθαρώτατα, ὅστις ὅτι μάλιστα αὐτῇ τῇ διανοίᾳ ἴοι ἐφ᾽ ἕκαστον,
μήτε τιν᾽ ὄψιν παρατιθέμενος ἐν τῷ διανοεῖσθαι μήτε τινὰ ἄλλην αἴσθησιν ἐφέλκων μετὰ τοῦ λογισμοῦ, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτῇ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν
εἰλικρινεῖ τῇ διανοίᾳ χρώμενος αὐτὸ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ εἰλικρινὲς ἕκαστον ἐπιχειροῖ θηρεύειν τῶν ὄντων, ἀπαλλαγεὶς ὅτι μάλιστα
ὀφθαλμῶν τε καὶ ὤτων καὶ ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν σύμπαντος τοῦ σώματος, ὡς ταράττοντος καὶ οὐκ ἐῶντος τὴν ψυχὴν κτήσασθαι ἀλήθειάν τε
καὶ φρόνησιν, ὅταν κοινωνῇ; ἆρ᾽ οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν, ὦ Σιμμία, εἴπερ τις καὶ ἄλλος, ὁ τευξόμενος τοῦ ὄντος; ὑπερφυῶς, ἔφη ὁ
Σιμμίας, ὡς ἀληθῆ λέγεις, ὦ Σώκρατες. οὐκοῦν ἀνάγκη, ἔφη, ἐκ πάντων τούτων παρίστασθαι δόξαν τοιάνδε τινὰ
τοῖς γνησίως φιλοσόφοις, ὥστε καὶ πρὸς ἀλλήλους τοιαῦτα ἄττα λέγειν, ὅτι κινδυνεύει τοι ὥσπερ ἀτραπός τις ἐκφέρειν
ἡμᾶς μετὰ τοῦ λόγου ἐν τῇ σκέψει, ὅτι, ἕως ἂν τὸ σῶμα ἔχωμεν καὶ συμπεφυρμένη ᾖ ἡμῶν ἡ ψυχὴ μετὰ τοιούτου
κακοῦ, οὐ μή ποτε κτησώμεθα ἱκανῶς οὗ ἐπιθυμοῦμεν· φαμὲν δὲ τοῦτο εἶναι τὸ ἀληθές. μυρίας μὲν γὰρ ἡμῖν
ἀσχολίας παρέχει τὸ σῶμα διὰ τὴν ἀναγκαίαν τροφήν· ἔτι δὲ ἄν τινες νόσοι προσπέσωσιν, ἐμποδίζουσιν ἡμῶν τὴν τοῦ ὄντος
θήραν. ἐρώτων δὲ καὶ ἐπιθυμιῶν καὶ φόβων καὶ εἰδώλων παντοδαπῶν καὶ φλυαρίας ἐμπίπλησιν ἡμᾶς πολλῆς.

do we say we know? For we say so, I suppose. Is it ever the case that we have learned this from someone, or not? Certainly, he said. And does it seem fitting to you for a man who is a philosopher to concern himself with such things as are called pleasures, for example, of foods and drinks? Not at all, Simmias said. What about sexual pleasures? Not at all.

And what about the other services to the body? Do you think they are honorable to such a person? For instance, the acquisition of expensive garments and footwear, and other bodily adornments; do you think he should value them or despise them, insofar as he is not strictly forced to partake of them? It seems to me he should despise them, he said, if he is a philosopher in truth.

Does it not seem to you, he said, that the entire business of such a man is not about the body, but rather, as much as he is able, he has turned away from it and toward the soul? It seems so to me. Is it not clear, then, first of all, that in such things the philosopher releases the soul as much as possible from communion with the body, in a way that distinguishes him from the rest of men? It appears so. And does it not seem, Simmias, to the majority of people that to one who finds nothing pleasant in such things, and does not partake of them, it is not worth living, but that such a person is close to being dead, as he cares nothing for the pleasures that come through the body? You speak very truly.

What, then, about the acquisition of wisdom itself? Is the body a hindrance or not, if one takes it along as a partner in the search? I mean something like this: do sight and hearing have any truth for men, or do the poets always din into our ears that we neither hear nor see anything accurately? Yet if these sensations of the body are neither accurate nor clear, the others are hardly so; for all of them are surely worse than these. Or do they not seem so to you? Certainly, he said.

When, then, he said, does the soul grasp the truth? For when it attempts to consider anything with the body, it is clear that it is then deceived by it. You speak truly. Is it not in reasoning, then, that something of the things that are <note>meaning the essences</note> becomes clear to it, if anywhere at all? Yes. And it surely reasons best then, when none of these things disturbs it, neither hearing nor sight nor pain nor any pleasure, but it becomes as much as possible all by itself, letting the body go, and as far as it can, neither sharing with it nor touching it, it reaches out for what is. These things are so. 

Does not the soul of the philosopher, therefore, especially despise the body and flee from it in this state, and seek to be all by itself? It appears so. But what of these things, Simmias? Do we say there is some Justice itself, or nothing? We do, by Zeus. And something Beautiful and Good? How could we not? Have you ever yet seen any such things with your eyes? Not at all, he said. But have you grasped them with any other sensation through the body? I speak of all things, such as magnitude, health, strength, and in a word, the essence of all other things—the true nature of what each happens to be. Is the most true nature of these things viewed through the body, or is it thus: whoever of us prepares himself most thoroughly and accurately to think about each thing he examines, he would come closest to knowing each one? Certainly.

Would he not do this most purely, who approaches each thing with his intellect alone, neither introducing any sight in his thinking, nor dragging in any other sense along with his reasoning, but using his pure intellect by itself, he attempts to hunt down each of the things that are, pure and alone, having departed as much as possible from eyes and ears, and, as one might say, the whole body, as it disturbs the soul and does not allow it to acquire truth and wisdom when it shares in it? Is this not the person, Simmias, if anyone, who will attain that which is? He spoke with extraordinary truth, said Simmias, as you say, Socrates.

Is it not necessary, he said, that from all these things, a conviction of such a kind should arise in genuine philosophers, so that they might say such things to one another, that there seems to be a sort of path that leads us, along with reason, in our reflection, that as long as we have the body and our soul is compounded with such an evil, we shall never sufficiently acquire what we desire? We say this is the truth. For the body provides us with countless distractions because of the necessary food; and if any diseases befall us, they hinder our hunt for what is. It fills us with loves, desires, fears, and images of all kinds, and much nonsense.

<meta>This page continues Socrates’ argument that philosophy is a preparation for death, specifically focusing on the purification of the soul.</meta>

So <gloss>if</gloss> we arrive where we hope, there <gloss>sufficiently</gloss>, if indeed anywhere <gloss>else</gloss>, we will possess that for the sake of which <gloss>the</gloss> great and <gloss>the</gloss> labor has been for us in our past life. So the <gloss>journey</gloss> now <gloss>enjoined</gloss> occurs with good hope <gloss>and</gloss> for another <gloss>of the</gloss> men who thinks he has prepared <gloss>for himself</gloss> his mind as if it were purified. "Exactly," said Simmias.

And is <gloss>to be</gloss> <term>purification<note>original: *katharsis* — the process of cleansing the soul from the body's influence to attain pure thought.</note></term> then not this very thing which has been said for a long time in the argument: the <gloss>and</gloss> separating of the soul from the body as much as possible, and habituating it <gloss>to</gloss> gather and collect from the body from all sides <gloss>toward</gloss> itself, and to dwell as far as possible both in the present and in the future alone by itself, released from the body as if from bonds? "Exactly," he said.

Then is this <gloss>itself</gloss> called death: the release and separation of soul from body? "Entirely <gloss>indeed</gloss>," <gloss>he said</gloss>. And those who are eager to release it, as we say, are always most of all and only those who practice philosophy correctly, and this <gloss>itself</gloss> is the very study of philosophers: the release and separation of soul from body. Or not? "It appears so." Therefore, as I was saying in the beginning, it would be ridiculous for a man who prepares himself in life to live as close as possible to being dead, to then be distressed when death comes to him?

<margin>The <unclear>explanation</unclear> of the truth is clear</margin>

How could he not? "In reality then, Simmias," he said, "those who practice philosophy correctly are training to die, and being dead is the least fearful thing to them among all men. Look at it from this: if they are hostile to the body in every way and desire to have the soul alone by itself, would it not be quite irrational if they were afraid and distressed when this happens, and did not go there gladly, to where there is hope for those who arrive to obtain what they loved through life—and they loved wisdom—and to be rid of that which they were hostile toward while it was with them?

Or if many, when human favorites and wives and sons died, were willing to go to <term>Hades<note>The Greek underworld; here Socrates refers to it as the place where the soul finds pure truth after death.</note></term> led by the hope that they would see and be with those they desired; will then someone who truly loves wisdom and has taken this same hope strongly—that he will meet it worthily nowhere else but in Hades—be distressed at dying and not go there gladly? One must think so, my friend, if he is truly a philosopher; for he will strongly believe this, that he will meet wisdom purely nowhere else but there. 

And if this is so, as I was just saying, would it not be quite irrational if such a man feared death? "Very much so, by Zeus," he said. "Then is this a sufficient sign for you of a man whom you see distressed when about to die, that he was not after all a philosopher, but some <term>lover-of-the-body<note>original: *philosomatos* — one who prioritizes physical existence and sensory pleasure over the soul.</note></term>? And this same person happens to be a lover-of-money and a lover-of-honor, either one of these or both."

"Exactly," he said, "it is so." "Then, Simmias," he said, "does not the so-called <term>courage<note>original: *andreia*.</note></term> belong most to these?" "Certainly," he said. "And also <term>temperance<note>original: *sophrosyne* — self-control or moderation of the desires.</note></term>, which even the many call temperance—not being fluttered by desires but being indifferent and orderly—does this not belong only to those who most disregard the body and live in philosophy?" "Necessarily," he said. "For if you are willing to consider the courage and temperance of others, it will seem strange to you." "How so, Socrates?"

"Because everyone," he said, "considers death to be among the great evils." "<gloss>The</gloss> very much so," he said.

<summary>Socrates explains that death is simply the separation of the soul from the body, a state that philosophers spend their lives practicing through the pursuit of wisdom. He argues that only a "lover of the body" would fear death, whereas a true philosopher welcomes the opportunity to find pure wisdom in the afterlife.</summary>

Hallelujah. Praise God.

When the testing <note>original: "nesyona"</note> of a human being occurs, he is summoned by the Great Judge <note>the Divine Judge</note> while you say: "My God." Since at that time <note>marker 1</note> he commanded the service, the majority at that time <note>marker 2</note> will be there. The witnesses <term>sahde</term> <gloss>witnesses or martyrs</gloss> <note>marker 3</note> alone will be tested, or they will be tested as if in a place <note>marker 4</note>. When he commands again, the witnesses shall teach, and with Hallelujah the witnesses shall be tested again. How then shall they be tested and how then shall they stand? Because of the witnesses again, and in his knowledge is the station <term>awan</term> <gloss>dwelling or stage</gloss> of witnesses. And how then shall they be tested? And how then shall they be tested? And in his knowledge are the witnesses then, and they and God, since then how then shall they be tested <note>marker 6</note> and how <note>marker 7</note> and how then shall they be tested. Because they were <note>marker 8</note> and God, how then shall they be tested, and how then shall they be tested, and how then shall the witnesses be tested, and how then shall they be tested:

### Discourse 20. Chapter 7.

It is that which is visible, which is of God, as He said, when the whole creation is not visible to it, but is given in the world of God. And they were, however, when it is given or given, or given <note>(1)</note> given: not, however, for the sake of the visible or given <note>(2)</note> given: not, however, for the sake of the visible or given: but the whole of it, the whole of it, is power. The standing of God, the commandment of God, and it is all given, and it is all given: that which is of all kings is given, from the God that is given <note>(3)</note> that is given: not given, and it became the whole of that which is given. When it is given, it is of God, when it is not given, when it is not given <note>(5)</note> given. The standing given <note>(6)</note> from that which is given: of that which is given, all to the king, as to God. Given: the whole of that which is given from that which is given: insights for the visible.

པདྨ་སམ་བྷ་ཝའི་མི་སློབ། །རྒུད་པའི་མས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རྣམ་མཁྱེན་མས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་མས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །མཐོང་བའི་ལམ་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །འདུ་བྱེད་པའི་ལམ་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ལམ་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །མིང་དང་གཟུགས་མས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །སྐྱེ་མཆེད་དྲུག་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རེག་པ་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །ཚོར་བའི་ལམ་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །སྲེད་པ་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །ལེན་པ་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །སྲིད་པ་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །སྐྱེ་བ་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རྒ་ཤི་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །རྒ་ཤི་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །སྐྱེ་བ་པས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །

གསོལ་བ་བཏབ་མེད་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །དེར་གསལ་མདུང་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རང་བཞིན་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རྟག་མཚན་ཉིད་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །མི་མིག་པས་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །དེས་སོ་མེད་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རྡོ་རྗེ་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །དེས་སོ་མེད་པའི་རྡོ་རྗེ་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རྣམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །ཨ་དག་པར་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་ཕན་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །དཔལ་རྣམ་པར་བཞག་པར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །སྤྲོས་བྲལ་མས་འཕེལ་བར་བྱ་བདང། །འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་མི་སློབ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ལམ་པར་

༄༅། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །འཕགས་པ་མཁའ་འགྲོ་མ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །འཕགས་པ་གནས་བརྟན་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །ཚེ་རིང་མཛད་རྣམ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །གསུང་རབ་མདོ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །འཕགས་པ་བསྟན་པའི་སློབ་པོ། །དྲམ་མཛད་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །མདོ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །མཚོན་མ་མཛད་དང་། །སློབ་མཛད་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །མཛོད་པས་ཤེས་པ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །འཕགས་པ་བསྟན་པའི་སློབ་པོ། །ཏིང་འཛིན་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །གསུང་རབ་ཀྱི་སློབ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་སློབ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སློབ་པོ།
